Pulmonary Disorders

Acute Asthma and Status Asthmaticus

Acute asthma is an airflow-obstruction emergency. The ED job is to reverse bronchospasm, treat inflammation early, measure response, and identify the patient who looks temporarily better but still has high relapse or death risk.

Board trap: A quiet chest is not reassuring in severe asthma; it can mean airflow is too low to generate wheeze.

ACUTE ASTHMA AND STATUS ASTHMATICUS

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder with episodic exacerbations caused by airway hyperresponsiveness. Attacks may resolve within minutes to hours, but many patients have chronic obstruction between episodes. Exacerbations are triggered by viral infections, allergens, tobacco smoke, pollution, occupational exposures, aspirin/NSAIDs in susceptible patients, emotional stress, weather, and medication nonadherence.

ED treatment begins before the cause is fully known. Early aggressive bronchodilator therapy and corticosteroids prevent respiratory failure, but disposition still depends on objective response and risk factors.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Asthma creates lower expiratory flow rates, air trapping, increased airway pressure, hypercarbia, hypoxemia, pulsus paradoxus, increased work of breathing, and possible ventilatory failure. Bronchospasm narrows airways acutely; edema, mucus, and inflammation extend the obstruction. Air trapping raises intrathoracic pressure and can impair venous return, especially when a fatigued patient is ventilated poorly or aggressively.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Typical symptoms include dyspnea, wheezing, cough, and chest tightness, but severity is judged by work of breathing, ability to speak, mental status, vital signs, oxygenation, and objective airflow when obtainable. Risk history matters: prior severe exacerbation, intubation, recent admission, frequent ED visits, poor adherence, SABA overuse, psychiatric disease, substance use, and low social support increase danger.

Clinical Course

Asthma severity is dynamic. Patients may initially improve after SABA and then worsen as inflammation and mucus persist. Classify severity and reassess after treatment; the one-hour objective response is more predictive than the first impression alone.

DIAGNOSIS AND PATIENT MONITORING

Diagnosis is usually clinical, but the ED must look for mimics and complications. Serial PEFR or FEV1 is useful when the patient can cooperate; a rising value supports response, while persistent low values drive admission or ICU care. Pulse oximetry follows oxygenation, and ABG/VBG is reserved for severe disease, fatigue, altered mental status, or suspected hypercapnia. Chest radiography, ECG, labs, and ultrasound are selective, not routine.

Pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, foreign body, vocal cord dysfunction, anaphylaxis, and upper-airway obstruction can all masquerade as asthma. Rosen's differential table reinforces this broader dyspnea frame.

ACUTE ASTHMA STANDARD TREATMENT

Standard treatment is repetitive or continuous inhaled SABA, oxygen titrated to adequate saturation, early systemic corticosteroids when response is not immediately complete, and ipratropium for moderate-to-severe exacerbations. The Tintinalli algorithm ties treatment intensity to severity and response, while Rosen emphasizes objective response categories and ED disposition consequences.

B-ADRENERGIC AGENTS

Inhaled beta2-Agonists

Inhaled beta2-agonists are first-line rescue therapy. Nebulizer and MDI-with-spacer delivery can both work; severe airflow obstruction often favors nebulized or continuous therapy because delivery by MDI may fail when inspiratory flow is poor. Do not underdose severe asthma because tachycardia appears; undertreatment is usually more dangerous than beta-agonist side effects.

CORTICOSTEROIDS

Systemic corticosteroids reduce relapse and hospitalization but take hours to reach maximal effect, so they should be given early. Oral prednisone/prednisolone is appropriate when tolerated; IV methylprednisolone is used when vomiting, severe distress, or impaired absorption makes oral therapy unreliable.

ANTICHOLINERGICS

Ipratropium is an adjunct to SABA in moderate-to-severe exacerbations and may reduce hospital admission. It is not a replacement for beta-agonist therapy and has limited chronic-control role in asthma. The treatment table belongs here because dosing is inseparable from the acute treatment discussion.

FOLLOW-UP OF PATIENTS WITH ACUTE ASTHMA

Disposition after acute treatment uses symptoms, exam, oxygenation, PEF/FEV1 response, prior history, medication access, adherence, and follow-up reliability. Good responders can often go home with SABA, corticosteroid plan when indicated, controller optimization, technique teaching, action plan, and follow-up in 1 to 4 weeks. Incomplete responders need observation or admission depending risk; poor responders need ongoing aggressive therapy and ICU consideration.

STATUS ASTHMATICUS (ACUTE SEVERE ASTHMA)

Status asthmaticus is acute severe asthma that fails to improve with usual inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. Findings include hypoxemia, tachypnea, tachycardia, accessory muscle use, exhaustion, altered mentation, and sometimes little or no wheezing. Rapid bronchodilation, early steroids, oxygenation, and timely escalation prevent arrest.

MAGNESIUM

IV magnesium sulfate is used for very severe exacerbations, especially when PEF/FEV1 is very low or response to initial therapy is poor. Hypotension is the main acute concern, so administer with monitoring.

NONINVASIVE POSITIVE-PRESSURE VENTILATION

NIPPV can reduce work of breathing in selected cooperative patients with severe asthma, but it must not delay intubation when mental status is altered, respiratory effort is failing, or arrest is near. Check for pneumothorax before starting when clinically suspected.

KETAMINE

Ketamine provides sedation and may bronchodilate, making it useful for RSI induction or procedural sedation in severe asthma. Evidence as a routine non-intubation adjunct is limited, but it remains a practical airway medication.

EPINEPHRINE

Epinephrine is standard for anaphylactic asthma and may be used in refractory severe bronchospasm when inhaled therapy is failing or cannot be delivered. It is not routine treatment for ordinary mild asthma exacerbation.

MECHANICAL VENTILATION

Intubate for cardiac or respiratory arrest, coma, severe altered consciousness, refractory hypoxemia, exhaustion, paradoxical breathing, or failed NIPPV. Mechanical ventilation does not directly relieve obstruction; it prevents arrest while bronchodilators and steroids work. Use permissive hypercapnia, low respiratory rate, long expiratory time, and close monitoring for dynamic hyperinflation and barotrauma.

AGENTS OF UNCERTAIN OR NO BENEFIT IN STATUS ASTHMATICUS

Heliox may lower airway resistance in selected refractory cases but is not routine. Aminophylline/theophylline are no longer first- or second-line because benefit is limited and toxicity is significant. Mast-cell stabilizers and leukotriene modifiers are controller or preventive therapies, not ED rescue drugs for acute bronchospasm.
